analysis.one_liner: Lets retirement advisers keep taking commissions while blocking stronger Labor Department conflict-of-interest rules.
analysis.headline: Two House committees approved the bill in early 2016, but the full House never voted on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a "best interest" standard for retirement investment advice into the tax code, but with large carve-outs: advisers could still recommend a limited menu of funds that includes their own firm's proprietary products, and could still be paid commissions, so long as the pay is "reasonable" and disclosed. At the same time, it would prohibit the Labor Department from ever tightening its own rules on retirement advice, and would block the Department's pending conflict-of-interest rule from taking effect unless Congress approved it within 60 days of enactment. In practice, the disclosure-based statutory standard would replace the stronger Department of Labor fiduciary rule that was being finalized at the time. The bill cleared two House committees but never reached the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Commission-based broker-dealers, insurance annuity sellers, and fund companies that sell proprietary products. The bill would exempt their transactions from the tax code's penalty on conflicted retirement advice as long as compensation is "reasonable" and disclosed, would allow advice limited to the adviser's own products, and would permanently freeze the Labor Department's authority to tighten conflict-of-interest rules while killing the stricter rule then in progress [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a definition of "best interest" advice in the tax code, requiring reasonable compensation, prudence, and putting the saver's interests above the adviser's, with liability if an adviser breaches it [S3] [S4] [S5].

Creates a remedy for savers: if advice fails the best-interest standard, the adviser must pay back the actual damages the saver suffered, on top of the tax code's excise tax on conflicted transactions [S4] [S5].

exempts best-interest advice and connected transactions from the prohibited-transaction tax, and allows advice based on a limited menu of investments that may include the adviser's own proprietary products, and advice that earns variable commissions, provided the limitations and compensation are disclosed before the transaction [S3] [S4] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Retirement savers in 401(k)s, IRAs, and similar accounts. They could continue paying commission-driven fees and receiving advice drawn from a limited menu of the adviser's own products, protected only by disclosures, and would lose the stronger Labor Department rule that this bill would have blocked from taking effect [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5].

drawbacks.text: A "best interest" recommendation may be based on a limited range of investment options, which may include the adviser's own proprietary products, and may earn the adviser variable commissions, as long as a notice says the same investments may be available elsewhere at a different cost [S3] [S4] [S5].

The bill prohibits the Labor Department from amending any of its investment-advice rules or positions, and any rule not in effect on January 1, 2015 — which covered the pending conflict-of-interest rule — could take effect only if Congress enacted a law specifically approving it within 60 days, effectively a kill switch for that rule [S2] [S3] [S4] [S5].

The best-interest standard allows an adviser to escape fault for errors or omissions in the required disclosures if the correction is made within 30 days of the adviser learning of the mistake [S4] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a real best-interest standard and a damages remedy with carve-outs that keep the commission and proprietary-product business model intact, and its most consequential provision is the one that goes the other way: it would have preempted the Labor Department's stricter conflict-of-interest rule with a weaker, disclosure-based statute, and barred the Department from ever tightening its rules again. An honest supporter would argue the statutory standard still imposes prudence and loyalty duties with real liability, and that the Department's rule threatened to raise compliance costs and push advisers away from small accounts; the honest weighing is that disclosure is a much weaker protection than a duty to avoid conflicts, and the 60-day kill switch for the Labor Department's rule shows where the bill's priority lay.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared both House committees in February 2016, was reported to the House and placed on the House calendar in April, and then sat there with no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Roskam introduced the bill on December 18, 2015, joined as original cosponsors by Democrats Richard Neal of Connecticut's John Larson, and Michelle Lujan Grisham, alongside Republicans [S5].
The House Ways and Means Committee ordered the bill reported, as amended, by a vote of 22-14 on February 2, 2016, and the Education and the Workforce Committee did so 26-12 the next day [S7].
On April 20, 2016 the bill was reported by both committees and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 392 [S7].
No further action was ever taken; the House never voted on the bill, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still on the calendar [S1] [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retirement savers came out ahead in the narrow sense that the bill never became law, so the Labor Department's stricter conflict-of-interest rule was not preempted by this statute and the Department's authority to tighten its rules was not permanently frozen. Commissioned advisers and annuity sellers lost their chance to lock in this statutory alternative before the rule took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retirement savers; the bill never passed

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (38 cosponsors split 32 Republican and 6 Democratic) and cleared two committees by votes of 22-14 and 26-12, but the record contains no recorded floor vote, so the partisan shape of the final outcome is unknown; the bill died by inaction.

industries.note: The bill would lock in the commission-based advice model by exempting conflicted transactions from the tax code's penalty so long as pay is "reasonable" and disclosed, and would bar the Labor Department from tightening its rules. Advisers could keep recommending their own firm's proprietary funds from a limited menu, so savers' protection would rest on disclosures rather than a duty to avoid conflicts.

The Labor Department's pending fiduciary rule threatened the high commissions on variable annuities sold into retirement accounts; this bill would have replaced it with a disclosure regime that allows variable (commission) compensation and preserves the sale.

Advisers who already avoid conflicts would face competition from commissioned sellers carrying the same statutory "best interest" label, eroding the distinction their business model depends on. The bill does not directly regulate them.
